newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: INTERVIEW-Venezuelan stats are fantasy-group chief.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Venezuelan stats are fantasy-group chief.

text.p: Trustworthy macroeconomic statistics do not exist in Venezuela, the newly appointed head of Congress' powerful Finance Commission said, adding that they are accounting "time bombs".
"The accounts (for the year) that the government has so far presented do not match reality," Carmelo Lauria, a member of opposition social democrat party Democratic Action (AD), told Reuters.
Venezuelan ministers have said they expect to end both this year and next in fiscal balance after the country posted a modest surplus in 1996 on high international oil prices.

But said Lauria, a former banker and one time government minister, said: "How can one make predictions about government spending in 1998 without having a clear idea about spending in 1997 first? They're creating false expectations.
"I sent a letter to the Finance Ministry asking for a reckoning of 1997's accounts," added Lauria, whose commission is the effective gatekeeper for all economic legislation.
"A month later, I still don't have any reply...the statistics backing up these claims don't exist."

Venezuela's budget process is traditionally less than transparent, analysts say. This year's budget for example has grown to 9.2 trillion bolivars from 7.8 trillion only a few months ago, largely due to a 75 percent public sector pay rise and pending social security reform expenses.

That extra spending is expected to erode much of last year's oil windfall of $3.8 billion, which was first earmarked for a Macroeconomic Stabilization Fund that would be drawn down during lean years of low oil prices and whose prudence had delighted investors.

A number of "accounting time bombs" further threaten the country's fiscal accounts, including some 500 billion bolivars ($1 billion) in tax refunds owed state-owned oil company PdVSA, and past due bills for goods and services totaling around 700 billion bolivars, he said.
Moreover, plans for the government gradually to pay-off its $3.8 billion debt with the Central Bank are stalled.
"The government is hiding all the bad stuff in the shade," Lauria said.

Analysts say Venezuelan government spending estimates are purposefully set low so as to deflect competing claims for budget funds, as well as allowing the government greater discretion to later spend over-budget revenues.
"I've been looking at proposed government budgets over the past 10 years and not once do they correspond to what was finally paid," Lauria said.
